I don't recommend The Emerald Maiden: Symphony of Dreams. It is a functional Hidden Object Mystery, but the puzzles are very easy and several of the story's twists turn out to simply be the main antagonist putting on a puppet show for the benefit of the protagonist. The aesthetics are generally good, with some nice underwater resort set pieces in the general vibe of Bioshock. There's a cool technician on staff who is half sea creature. I just... don't feel that the plot holds together very well.

There's two simulated areas based on the home of a low-contact South American tribe, both with Hidden Object Puzzles featuring items from Africa, such as tiger and elephant statues. The first area was short and seemed more of a recreation of a dream sequence, so I gave it some slack. The second area was more grounded, so the items from tribal cultures around the world came across as being more out of place.

The bonus chapter is good, and helps ground the main story in reality, by revealing who funded the protagonist's trip to the submerged hotel, and how the place was still stocked with supplies years past the disappearance of the protagonist's family. That said, the fetch quests in the bonus chapter are resolved with items found in some pretty absurd locations. Plus, the protagonist doesn't want to break a lot of things throughout the game, but is somehow suddenly fine with shooting a cannon into a storefront...

I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you.

[u]Recommendation[/u]: Another fun hidden-object game from Artifex Mundi that has a lot of superficial similarities with the setting of [u]Bioshock[/u].

[u]Critique[/u]: At first, this seems to have less in common with other Artifex Mundi hidden object games: even though you play a female protagonist, use coins as screwdrivers, do lots of the same puzzles, it somehow feels fresh because of the mid-century science fiction aesthetic and the fact that the people that you interact with early in the game are crude holographic recordings of people rather than the people themselves. Having a justification for why one is creeped out by the uncanny valley is [i]great[/i] here. Unfortunately, that breaks down by the end of the game, when you run into real people with horrible animations, and discover that there is still a supernatural menace after all. A lot of Artifex Mundi games have fantastically twisted, Byzantine plots, and to me that's a strength. This game is no exception: the plot is an amusement park ride where you don't know how the story will develop as you reach each milestone.

The other fun/funny bit is that this is one of the Artifex Mundi subgenre of games in which you have a little NPC "helper" that helps you get things you can't reach or interact with on your own. In some games it's a squirrel or a bird. In this one, it's a little robot helper that flies around with a propeller head, then [i]uses its face to unlock doors[/i]! It's hysterical, watching your little robot buddy awkwardly face-plant to open doors/activate switches: a little bit of slapstick in an otherwise very melodramatic game.

[u]Review[/u]: [spoiler]Back in the 1950s, fear of the Cold War sparked a brain trust of paranoid scientists to create an undersea refuge from the world. You - an orphaned girl - have finally discovered the location of this sea base, and the game begins as you arrive and begin to try to trick or satisfy the automated systems of the base so that you can enter. You discover that, for the most part, there are no people left on the base, but it is possible to continue your detective work by using the systems on the base, which include "dream" recordings: alternative worlds that you can enter if you find the requisite discs. In the process, you find that your father was one of the masterminds of this dream park. Miraculously, it seems that your father is still alive, living as a sort of sinister "phantom of the opera" figure, setting up traps and sabotaging systems to try to drive you off. But eventually you find the source of the dream park technology: an ancient spirit that was plundered from the Amazon. She has been puppeting your father for decades, and now wants to take over your body! With the help of some hideously mutated survivors (straight out of Davy Jones' crew from the [u]Pirates of the Caribbean[/u] movies), you have to figure out how to defeat the evil spirit and free your father from his eternal bondage.[/spoiler]

This was a great hidden-object game.  The text-adventure made sense without any leaps of Bat-Logic needed; if you needed to open a door you had to find a key, not a bottle of aspirin and a pair of cymbals like in some Artifex Mundi games.  The store was easy to follow and actually made sense, and all the puzzles and mini-games were both different than the usual sliding puzzles and interesting and all were solvable without a hint guide.   Additionally, there was a nice variety of hidden-object scenes: some were the standard checklist of find a dozen items, but some required you to put items together based on silhouettes or assemble an object using parts hidden around the hidden-object screen.  

As with many such games, you had to find one extra hidden object per scene-- in this case, a rose-- but as roses are red, they were all easily found.   

Note for achievement hunters: all are doable and acquirable, but quite a few are optional and thus missable, so if you're a perfectionist check a guide or the discussion forums before you start as there are things you might not consider doing.  There's a bonus chapter but it is short and has no achievements.

An average hidden object game that is fully voice-acted and animated.

Graphics are a bit dated but overall, the game looks decent. The backgrounds, locations, and characters are mostly bland and uninteresting. Shockingly, some hidden object scenes seem to have glitched or unfinished backgrounds with missing parts and badly cut image elements.

Sounds are OK, but some tracks have been reused from another game of the publisher, Abyss: The Wraiths of Eden.

The story and ambience are average and do not really manage to keep the player's interest. There are several points that needed some kind of explanation but the game just did not want to address these.

Some of the required actions are incomprehensible; for example, the player is asked by one of the side-characters to push a button - except there is no button, it must be found first. But then why not ask the player to find the button instead?

With the exception of some minigames, the game is very easy.

The collectibles and achievements are hard to miss, with the exception of one. There is also a bonus chapter that continues the story but does not conclude it.

Surprisingly, there are inconsistencies in the game; for example, the hidden object scene asks for a 'spyglass' but the item to find is actually a hand glass.

If you prefer the hidden object portion of Artifex's typical HOG's, and don't mind a patchwork story with early portions ripped directly from Bioshock, then this one's for you. It's almost like the artists and writers just stitched together assets from three incomplete games. Anyway, as with all of these Artifex games, they're absolutely not worth full price, and should be picked up when they go on sale every two months or so.

Vierge D'Émeraude : Une symphonie de Rêves est un jeu point & clic de style HOG, dans lequel nous recevons une mystérieuse invitation dans un complexe sous-marin. A la recherche de réponses et de vérités, nous allons devoir affronter les dangers qui rodent, dans ce lieu étrange et tenter de survivre. C'est un très bon jeu, avec une bonne ambiance et une histoire intéressante. Un épisode bonus, qui fait suite à l'histoire, viendra rallonger un peu, la durée de l'aventure.

The Emerald Maiden: Symphony of Dreams is a hidden object game where you play as a woman who travels into a mysterious undersea facility called Emerald Maiden on a mission to find her real parents. The main attraction of the facility is the Dream Machine, which allows people to visit dreams. To be honest, what caught my interest is the BioShock-like premise, although the facility here is still in a pretty pristine condition and not ruined. I was kinda worried the game would take too much place in the dreams, but luckily this isn't the case. The dreams feel more like short side rooms.

What I like most about this game is the free-roam levels. Most HOGs are linear, with places locking out after a bit. However, here it all takes place inside the facility and some dreams, and you can revisit all of the places (except one) freely after you unlock them. Useful if you missed one of the rose collectibles, or simply if you want to look around. It is a feature that more HOGs should use, especially since good artstyles that are pleasing to look at is the main strength of this genre. After you finish the story, you can play the extra game mode, which acts as an epilogue. It's short and the map is free-roam too.

The subtitles in this game seem to be a bit broken. There are plenty of typos, which is unusual in games. Some "failed interaction" objects also don't give a clue what to do, like there's the interaction button but no subtitles about what should be done here. I'm also not a fan of the fact how some puzzles, especially the more difficult "sliding" ones, have no reset buttons. And lastly, while the artstyle of the game is beautiful, the ones in the extra game looks noticeably worse. Like it's so low-res and with washed-out colors.

In conclusion, The Emerald Maiden: Symphony of Dreams is a pretty good HOG, mostly due to the setting and especially the free-roam map which more HOGs should implement. However, if you want a more, BioShock-y HOG I'd recommend Abyss: The Wraiths of Eden as the city there is ruined and overgrown as well. I recommend giving both games a try if you want nice HOGs or need some games to fill that BioShock-shaped void.

Huh... someone at Artifex Mundi must've really liked Bioshock... xD

Like Abyss: The Wraiths of Eden, the inspiration here is kinda obvious.
Well, at least on a few elements... of course neither this one nor Abyss were total copies of Bioshock, but there's a lot of borrowing elements from it. It's just the setup that is interesting as in a utopic city for rich people built deep under the sea in a secretive way using forbidden or obscure ancient tech - gonne wrong.

Anyways, this one looks more along the modern hidden object games.
The graphics are great, more or less along with the newer crop of games with hidden object parts, scenarios and whatnot that fits together better than the older games. It feels somewhere between the older Artifex Mundi games, and the newer crop.

The mechanics and flow of the game though... man, I don't think any of the other hidden object games had such a bad flow. Mechanics are basic - there is one collectable distributed at random scenes, which I don't like much. It's a single rose, and not multiple different things, which is a good thing for me. But there is no indication if there is one in the scene or not, some are very well hidden, and since they don't appear in every single scene, you're not sure if you should look for one or not. At least there aren't too many of them.

But the flow of the game is the worst part. The game never locks past scenes, and there is a whole ton of things you need to collect to advance from the beginning of the game onwards... so you are constantly with incomplete sets of objects or tools lingering in your inventory because you'll really only use or find all that are needed way later in the game.

There are a few areas and hidden object scenes that are there, but they only unlock after you've done all possible actions previous to it, which is not a great way to make the game more difficult... you see what you need in a hidden object part, but you don't get it. It's like, look at it, it's right there, pick it up, nope, ok. Need to wait for whenever the game decides to unlock the hidden object part again.

As you travel inside different scenarios in dreams, the constant backtracking is innevitable, but made even harder because there are loads of times you are unsure what the next step should be. Like I said, you are holding a bunch of different sets of things, plus tools that could have multiple different usages, so it's hard to guess what you need to get to unlock the next part - there is no sequential logic.

A few of the scenes hide some necessary tools for advancing in the scene, and the place you have to click to zoom into the specific area is too close to another, so it can be hard to spot. So, for instance, the shovel close to the truck, the radio between the entrance of the vivarium and the robot upgrade thing, stuff like that. Makes it hard to figure out what is something you need to take a closer look, or just part of the scenario.

It's still an ok game though, if you are tolerant enough. With these games, specially if you are just getting into them, you gotta keep in mind that there was a steady evolution of concepts, stories, mechanics and whatnot to get to the point it's currently at. So, while it may be a bit jarring to play a newer title and then go for an older one, it's interesting to see the evolution of it.
